sections.title: A managed search—not a promise of employment.

The exact activities and approvals are defined in the engagement. Employers retain control of interviews, selection and offers; KOV does not guarantee interviews, placement or timing.

sections.title: Set a target that respects your constraints.
paragraphs: Before execution, KOV and the professional discuss seniority, function, industry, geography, timing and practical requirements. Search boundaries can include current-employer exclusions, location constraints and communication preferences.
This makes it possible to focus on roles that fit your priorities rather than measuring progress by application volume alone.

Record organization and role exclusions

Establish reporting and review preferences

sections.title: Keep the process visible and the decisions yours.

Fees, deliverables and expectations are discussed directly by message and agreed in writing before work begins. Client information is shared only according to the agreed communication process.

faqs.question: Is reverse recruiting the same as an employer hiring a recruiter?
faqs.answer: No. In KOV's candidate practice, the professional engages KOV for agreed job-search support. Employers make their own hiring decisions and are not represented by this candidate-side service.

faqs.question: Does reverse recruiting guarantee a job?
faqs.answer: No. KOV can manage agreed search activities, but cannot control employer decisions, market conditions or hiring timelines.

Prepare concise answers to likely questions

sections.title: From sector to the specific activity of an establishment
paragraphs: The North American Industry Classification System groups establishments by economic activity. Its hierarchy moves from sectors to subsectors, industry groups, and industry codes. The Census Bureau's 2022 structure workbook contains 20 sector headings, 96 subsectors, 308 industry groups, 689 five-digit NAICS industries, and 1,012 six-digit U.S. national industries. The five-digit and six-digit counts describe distinct levels; neither should be substituted for the other.

The workbook presents three sector ranges as grouped rows: Manufacturing (31-33), Retail Trade (44-45), and Transportation and Warehousing (48-49). Those are three rows in the structure file but represent nine two-digit sectors in the 20-sector total. The full official codes and titles are listed in the table above. A marker in the source title indicates trilateral agreement and is preserved as a note in this directory.

Classification is based on establishment activity, not simply the brand name, job title, or every product a company sells. A diversified organization may include establishments with different activities. When a code matters, check the official definitions and apply the classification rules to the establishment being described rather than inferring a code from a marketing label.

Use the hierarchy to narrow research. Start with a broad sector, identify the relevant subsector and industry group, then review both five-digit and six-digit codes where U.S. national detail matters. Parent codes help show how an activity fits into the larger structure. This supports consistent terminology in market research, resumes, and career conversations, but it does not measure how many employers or jobs exist in a category.

The current first-batch detail pages provide deeper directories for Professional, Scientific, and Technical Services; Finance and Insurance; Information; and Health Care and Social Assistance. Other sectors remain visible in the official top-level listing and will receive detail pages in subsequent verified batches. No missing sector URL is presented as live until its page has been built and checked.

sections.title: Industry context informs a career decision; it does not decide it
paragraphs: A leadership title can conceal a different operating reality from one sector to another. Before comparing opportunities, document the employer's business model, customer or beneficiary, revenue or funding context, operating footprint, governance, and the actual role mandate. Then identify which parts of your experience transfer and what evidence a new audience will need.

Market comparisons should be treated as research questions rather than generic country rankings. Validate the employing entity, local requirements, work authorization, decision authority, and current employer facts using dated sources. The same sector code does not guarantee the same regulation, hiring process, compensation, or role scope across countries.

A useful career brief records the target role, industry codes where relevant, acceptable adjacent sectors, exclusions, location constraints, and evidence needed to support the move. This keeps the search specific while leaving room to recognize credible alternatives.

sections.title: Major groups organize occupations by the work performed
paragraphs: The 2018 Standard Occupational Classification organizes occupations into major groups, minor groups, broad occupations, and detailed occupations. The official BLS structure and definitions workbooks contain 23 major groups, 98 minor groups, 459 broad occupations, and 867 detailed occupations. This hub lists all major groups; the classification is useful for consistent reference, but it is not a directory of employer job titles.

The hierarchy helps readers narrow from a broad occupational family to a more specific description. The detailed definition is the most useful check when titles vary or a role combines several kinds of work. A code should be selected based on responsibilities and the official classification rules, not merely because a title sounds similar.

The major group table reproduces the official SOC code and title. Each group contains a different number of subordinate occupations. The SOC 2018 structure and definitions files are both included in the local source directory; the detailed occupation definitions have been checked against the structure codes and titles.

Management, Legal, Business and Financial Operations, and Computer and Mathematical are among the first occupation-group pages with full official directories. They show how one major group branches into its minor, broad, and detailed occupations. Other groups remain in the top-level listing until their own detail pages are built and validated.

SOC is not a seniority scale. A detailed occupation can describe work performed at different levels, while one executive title may combine responsibilities from several occupational families. To describe a senior role, pair the SOC concept with the employer's mandate, reporting line, decision rights, team and budget scope, and the outcomes for which the person was accountable.

sections.title: Executive titles do not replace occupational analysis
paragraphs: A title such as CEO, CFO, CTO, partner, or vice president may draw on more than one occupational family. Use the duties, reporting relationship, and actual accountability to describe the work; the examples below are not extra SOC codes.

sections.title: Use occupational codes alongside industry and employer context
paragraphs: A person's occupation and an organization's industry answer different questions. SOC describes the work performed; NAICS describes the establishment's economic activity. One employer can hire people across many SOC groups, and the same occupation can appear in many industries. Comparing both dimensions can make target research clearer without implying that a code alone captures an entire role.

For career planning, identify the tasks and decisions that define the target role, then compare them with your own evidence. Include relevant professional credentials, team leadership, functional scope, operating context, and constraints. If a move crosses occupational groups, explain the bridge rather than relying on a title match.

Market observations must be current and local. Validate role requirements, licensing, work authorization, reporting relationships, and employer-specific titles directly. The directory makes no claim about current vacancies or the relative demand for any occupation.

sections.title: How this sector is organized and led
paragraphs: NAICS 54 covers a wide range of establishments whose primary activity is providing specialized professional, scientific, or technical services. The sector's breadth is visible in its nine subsectors, which include professional services such as legal and accounting, architecture and engineering, design, computer-related services, consulting, research, advertising, and other specialist activities. A code describes an establishment's primary economic activity; it does not describe every service that the organization offers or every role it employs.

Leadership in a knowledge-service organization often involves balancing expertise, client trust, delivery quality, and commercial sustainability. The actual balance differs substantially between a regulated professional practice, a project-based technical consultancy, a research organization, and a large multi-service firm. A senior title alone therefore provides little evidence of scale. Useful context includes client type, project size, recurring versus one-off work, the delivery model, the degree of professional regulation, and the leader's authority over people, pricing, and risk.

Hiring processes in this sector can be mandate-led: an employer may need someone to deepen a technical practice, expand a client portfolio, improve delivery discipline, lead a geographic team, or integrate a service after organizational change. Those are possible search questions, not claims that any particular market currently has demand. Candidates should identify which business problem they have actually addressed and support the claim with verifiable examples, while protecting confidential client information.

Career transitions can cross subsector boundaries when the candidate can explain how their expertise transfers. A leader moving from a specialist advisory practice into an in-house role may need to translate client-facing recommendations into ownership of internal execution. Someone moving from a technical delivery business to a broader services company may need to show how they managed cross-functional teams, service economics, quality controls, and customer outcomes. The classification helps organize research but does not establish role equivalence.

A strong industry narrative connects the work performed to the operating environment. It identifies the services delivered, who relied on them, the complexity and constraints involved, the leader's decisions, and what changed as a result. Avoid describing a whole firm as belonging to one subsector without checking its primary activity. Equally, avoid presenting the NAICS label as proof of expertise: a professional's work history and specific responsibilities remain the evidence for a credible senior-career story.

The sector also includes organizations with different talent and governance models: sole or small practices, partner-led firms, project consultancies, research establishments, and larger networks. A senior candidate should identify how the target earns or funds its work, whether client relationships belong to an individual or a firm, and how quality is reviewed. These distinctions affect the meaning of business development, utilization, practice leadership, and succession. They should be researched for the specific organization rather than assumed from the NAICS code.

Technology and automation can change how a professional service is delivered, but a claim about innovation should identify the underlying work. Explain whether you selected systems, changed a process, led a product or service, improved review and quality, or simply used a tool within a team. For advisory or research work, describe methods and decision influence without disclosing confidential client material. Employers need to understand both the expertise involved and the candidate's accountability for implementing or governing it.

Some senior professionals consider moving into a board, advisory, or independent consulting portfolio. Those paths involve different expectations for independence, conflicts, time commitment, fiduciary obligations, and business development. They should not be presented as automatic next steps from practice leadership. A candidate considering one should examine the appointment or engagement terms, the organization’s governance, and any professional duties that continue to apply.

In every comparison, keep the establishment classification separate from the professional's own occupation. A consulting firm can employ lawyers, analysts, engineers, software specialists, and executives at the same time; the NAICS code describes its business activity, not the whole workforce.

sections.title: Assess a transition through this sector
paragraphs: A move from engineering consultancy leadership into a national practice role requires evidence of technical quality, client development, team leadership, and delivery across disciplines. Compare the target firm's service mix and the role's authority before treating prior experience as a match.

A disciplined preparation would map the target firm's actual service mix, identify which of the candidate's projects are comparable, establish team and budget scope, and prepare examples of quality decisions, client outcomes, and collaboration across disciplines. The candidate would also test the new role's authority, professional requirements, and expectations before approving any outreach.

sections.title: How this sector is organized and led
paragraphs: Finance and Insurance (NAICS 52) brings together several business models: monetary authorities and depository institutions, credit intermediation and related activities, securities and investment activity, insurance carriers, agencies and brokerages, and funds or other financial vehicles. These are not interchangeable settings. Each can place different weight on funding, assets, distribution, underwriting, customer relationships, technology, controls, and regulatory obligations. The directory's hierarchy is a reliable starting point for naming the employer's activity more precisely.

Senior leadership scope is best understood through the decisions owned. For a finance executive, that may involve capital allocation, liquidity, planning, reporting, or investor communication; for a risk leader, it may involve risk appetite, controls, remediation, or governance; for a business leader, it may center on a product, customer segment, or distribution channel. These are role lenses rather than universal definitions. The job description, reporting line, and applicable regulator determine the actual remit.

The sector makes evidence and trust especially important in a career narrative. Candidates should explain the scale and context of decisions, the safeguards applied, and their own contribution. Avoid unsupported claims about assets, portfolio performance, compliance outcomes, customer growth, or regulatory standing. If figures are confidential or were produced by a team, state the boundaries and attribute the work accurately.

A transition between financial subsectors can be possible when the leader can connect common capabilities—such as governance, customer service, data, or enterprise operations—to the new business model. It still requires careful testing. A leader from insurance distribution may not have the same experience as someone accountable for underwriting or claims. A finance executive in a corporate treasury role is not automatically interchangeable with a senior leader in a regulated financial institution.

Market comparisons should focus on the actual employing entity, permission to operate, product, customers, role authority, and applicable jurisdiction. A global organization can have locally distinct entities and responsibilities. Use official employer disclosures and regulator registers when relevant, and seek qualified legal or compliance advice for questions outside career representation. This page provides classification context, not regulatory advice or current hiring data.

The sector includes both institutions that hold or intermediate financial assets and organizations that support financial activity, as well as insurance businesses and investment vehicles. The exact boundaries matter when a role description refers to balance-sheet accountability, product governance, customer suitability, underwriting, or portfolio oversight. Candidates should identify the legal entity and the business line they served. Where an organization has multiple regulated subsidiaries, explain which one employed the candidate and where their authority began and ended.

Data, technology, and operational resilience are increasingly visible in financial leadership discussions, but candidates should not use these themes as generic claims. Specify the system or process, business owners, risks addressed, and the candidate's role in approving or delivering the change. If an initiative involved third-party providers or shared services, distinguish governance and oversight from direct engineering or operational ownership. This precision supports credible conversations with boards, regulators, and hiring leaders.

Financial achievements need careful attribution. Revenue, investment returns, loss reduction, customer acquisition, and capital outcomes may depend on markets, teams, and external conditions. A candidate can describe decisions, controls, and contribution without claiming sole causation. When using metrics, preserve context and confidentiality and be ready to explain the measurement period. This is especially important when a transition crosses asset classes, financial products, or regulated entities.

A precise description also helps distinguish corporate finance experience from work inside a financial intermediary or insurer. State the entity, product, and control environment before drawing conclusions about transferability; avoid treating a familiar title as evidence of identical accountability. For senior searches, document who approved key decisions and how oversight worked, without disclosing restricted information.

sections.title: How this sector is organized and led
paragraphs: The Information sector (NAICS 51) includes establishments associated with publishing, motion pictures and sound recording, broadcasting, telecommunications, data processing and hosting, and other information services. The official hierarchy distinguishes these activities rather than treating all digital or media businesses as one industry. A platform company, a connectivity provider, a content producer, and a data-hosting business may share technology and customers yet operate under different business models and constraints.

Leadership roles in information businesses can sit at the intersection of content, product, infrastructure, customer experience, revenue, and risk. The relevant balance depends on the specific establishment and role. For example, a technology executive may own internal systems, a customer platform, network operations, or product engineering; a commercial leader may focus on advertising, subscriptions, enterprise accounts, or distribution. Candidates should use the job mandate—not the sector label—to define what they have led.

Business changes in information organizations can make the boundaries between disciplines less obvious. A senior candidate may have led a digital transition within a traditional publisher or content strategy within a technology business. The strongest evidence separates what changed, who made the decisions, which teams were involved, how customers or users were affected, and which results can be supported. Avoid vague claims such as 'transformed digital' without showing the work and the level of accountability.

A career transition across subsectors can require translating operating context. Infrastructure reliability, editorial independence, content rights, data stewardship, advertising economics, and product iteration are different concerns; not every role carries each one. Candidates should identify which of these they have actually managed and where a new employer's requirements may differ. The six-digit U.S. classification detail can help name an establishment's activity, but does not prove a particular role is comparable.

For cross-border searches, establish the employing entity, customer base, service footprint, and exact role before interpreting the market. A global brand can have local operations with distinct authority and priorities. Current employment conditions and legal requirements must be checked with up-to-date, jurisdiction-specific sources. NAICS codes are stable reference labels for the 2022 edition, not a real-time description of every organization's portfolio or current hiring plans.

The Information sector is not synonymous with the entire technology economy. Establishment classification follows defined economic activity, while product portfolios and modern business models can span classifications. A company may offer software, content, advertising, connectivity, or data services from different entities. For a senior search, map the target's real business and customer proposition, then describe the role against that operating context. If the public NAICS code is not known, state the uncertainty rather than assigning one from a brand description.

Leadership evidence in this environment benefits from clear product and operational boundaries. State whether you were accountable for discovery, roadmaps, editorial or rights decisions, service availability, network performance, customer operations, or internal systems. Explain key dependencies and decision forums. A digital product may connect several functions without giving one leader authority over all of them, so describe collaboration and escalation honestly rather than implying complete ownership.

Cross-border work can introduce distinct issues around content rights, privacy, security, infrastructure location, communications permissions, or service availability. Not every role is responsible for those matters, and requirements vary by activity and jurisdiction. Candidates should identify which responsibilities they held and which belonged to legal, security, or regulatory teams. For a target role, check current official requirements and the employer's own disclosures before presenting a market or compliance claim.

Because services and products can cross conventional boundaries, record the source and date of any industry mapping. If a target's primary activity is unclear, keep the classification provisional and focus the career discussion on the role's actual products, customers, and operating responsibilities.

sections.title: How this sector is organized and led
paragraphs: Health Care and Social Assistance (NAICS 62) includes ambulatory health care services, hospitals, nursing and residential care facilities, and social assistance. The activities differ in how services are delivered, how organizations are structured, and which professionals, communities, or institutions they serve. Classification gives a common language for describing establishment activity, but the code alone cannot tell a reader whether a provider is public, private, nonprofit, large, small, or integrated with other services.

Senior leadership in this sector can involve a broad set of operational and professional considerations: service access, workforce capacity, quality, safety, finance, technology, facilities, patient or client experience, and governance. The exact accountability depends on the organization and job. A clinical leader may have professional responsibilities not held by a general operations executive; a social assistance organization may have a different delivery model from a hospital or outpatient group. Candidates must state their remit accurately.

Hiring for leadership roles may be shaped by a specific organizational challenge, such as improving access, coordinating services, stabilizing operations, upgrading systems, or strengthening governance. These are common mandate questions, not claims about current vacancies. A candidate should be ready to explain the conditions under which their experience was gained, what constraints applied, and what outcomes they personally influenced. Where outcomes depend on care teams or external funding, attribute contributions carefully.

Career transitions between health settings can be valuable but require context. Experience in a single-site clinical environment may not directly demonstrate leadership across a multi-site network; a social service executive may bring strong community delivery experience but need to show how it maps to a regulated clinical organization. Senior professionals should identify transferable capabilities and make non-transferable credentials or experience gaps visible early.

For international moves, confirm how the role is classified by the employer, what professional registration or authorization is required, and whether the role is clinical, operational, corporate, or advisory. Requirements vary by jurisdiction and profession, so rely on the relevant official regulator and qualified advisers. This directory is a NAICS reference only and does not provide clinical, licensing, legal, or employment advice.

The classification combines establishments with different service and funding arrangements. A hospital, outpatient practice, residential facility, and community assistance provider can have different governance, professional roles, capital needs, and measures of service. An executive comparing them should identify who receives the service, how it is delivered, which entities control it, and which external bodies influence requirements. The NAICS hierarchy helps name the establishment category, while organization-specific research reveals how the service operates.

Workforce planning, capacity, and service continuity are recurring leadership questions in care and support settings, but candidates should anchor any example in a specific mandate. Explain the baseline, constraints, decisions, and contribution of multidisciplinary partners. Quality or safety statements require particular care: describe the governance process and evidence accurately, and do not imply clinical authority if the role was operational or administrative. Confidential patient, client, employee, and provider information must remain protected.

Technology change can affect scheduling, records, care coordination, analytics, and service access. An executive who led a digital program should clarify their relationship to clinicians, service users, privacy teams, vendors, and operational owners. A transformation result is stronger when it describes implementation and adoption as well as system selection. If outcome evidence is sensitive or not independently attributable, present the process and scope without overstating a clinical or social result.

Keep establishment classification separate from profession and licensure. The same provider can employ clinicians, administrators, technology leaders, finance professionals, and social-service teams; the NAICS code does not describe each person's role or qualify anyone to deliver care. Use those distinctions when reviewing a target's role requirements.

entries.definition: Develop, introduce, or enact laws and statutes at the local, tribal, state, or federal level. Includes only workers in elected positions.

entries.name: Advertising, Marketing, Promotions, Public Relations, and Sales Managers
Advertising and Promotions Managers
entries.definition: Plan, direct, or coordinate advertising policies and programs or produce collateral materials, such as posters, contests, coupons, or giveaways, to create extra interest in the purchase of a product or service for a department, an entire organization, or on an account basis.

entries.name: Marketing Managers
entries.definition: Plan, direct, or coordinate marketing policies and programs, such as determining the demand for products and services offered by a firm and its competitors, and identify potential customers. Develop pricing strategies with the goal of maximizing the firm’s profits or share of the market while ensuring the firm’s customers are satisfied. Oversee product development or monitor trends that indicate the need for new products and services.

entries.name: Sales Managers
entries.definition: Plan, direct, or coordinate the actual distribution or movement of a product or service to the customer. Coordinate sales distribution by establishing sales territories, quotas, and goals and establish training programs for sales representatives. Analyze sales statistics gathered by staff to determine sales potential and inventory requirements and monitor the preferences of customers.

entries.name: Public Relations Managers
entries.definition: Plan, direct, or coordinate activities designed to create or maintain a favorable public image or raise issue awareness for their organization or client.

entries.name: Fundraising Managers
entries.definition: Plan, direct, or coordinate activities to solicit and maintain funds for special projects or nonprofit organizations.

entries.name: Administrative Services Managers
entries.definition: Plan, direct, or coordinate one or more administrative services of an organization, such as records and information management, mail distribution, and other office support services. Medical records administrators are included in “Medical and Health Services Managers” (11-9111). Excludes “Facilities Managers” (11-3013) and “Purchasing Managers” (11-3061).

entries.name: Facilities Managers
entries.definition: Plan, direct, or coordinate operations and functionalities of facilities and buildings. May include surrounding grounds or multiple facilities of an organization’s campus. Excludes “Administrative Services Managers” (11-3012), “Property, Real Estate, and Community Association Managers” (11-9141), “First-Line Supervisors of Building and Grounds Cleaning and Maintenance Workers” (37-1010), “First-Line Supervisors of Mechanics and Repairers” (49-1011), and “Maintenance and Repair Workers, General” (49-9071).

entries.name: Computer and Information Systems Managers
entries.definition: Plan, direct, or coordinate activities in such fields as electronic data processing, information systems, systems analysis, and computer programming. Excludes “Computer Occupations” (15-1211 through 15-1299).

entries.name: Financial Managers
entries.definition: Plan, direct, or coordinate accounting, investing, banking, insurance, securities, and other financial activities of a branch, office, or department of an establishment. Excludes “Financial Risk Specialists” (13-2054).

entries.name: Industrial Production Managers
entries.definition: Plan, direct, or coordinate the work activities and resources necessary for manufacturing products in accordance with cost, quality, and quantity specifications.

entries.name: Purchasing Managers
entries.definition: Plan, direct, or coordinate the activities of buyers, purchasing officers, and related workers involved in purchasing materials, products, and services. Includes wholesale or retail trade merchandising managers and procurement managers.

entries.name: Transportation, Storage, and Distribution Managers
entries.definition: Plan, direct, or coordinate transportation, storage, or distribution activities in accordance with organizational policies and applicable government laws or regulations. Includes logistics managers.

entries.name: Compensation and Benefits Managers
entries.definition: Plan, direct, or coordinate compensation and benefits activities of an organization. Job analysis and position description managers are included in “Human Resources Managers” (11-3121).

entries.name: Human Resources Managers
entries.definition: Plan, direct, or coordinate human resources activities and staff of an organization. Excludes managers who primarily focus on compensation and benefits (11-3111) and training and development (11-3131).

entries.name: Training and Development Managers
entries.definition: Plan, direct, or coordinate the training and development activities and staff of an organization.

entries.name: Farmers, Ranchers, and Other Agricultural Managers
Farmers, Ranchers, and Other Agricultural Managers
entries.definition: Plan, direct, or coordinate the management or operation of farms, ranches, greenhouses, aquacultural operations, nurseries, timber tracts, or other agricultural establishments. May hire, train, and supervise farm workers or contract for services to carry out the day-to-day activities of the managed operation. May engage in or supervise planting, cultivating, harvesting, and financial and marketing activities. Excludes “First-Line Supervisors of Farming, Fishing, and Forestry Workers” (45-1011).

entries.name: Construction Managers
entries.definition: Plan, direct, or coordinate, usually through subordinate supervisory personnel, activities concerned with the construction and maintenance of structures, facilities, and systems. Participate in the conceptual development of a construction project and oversee its organization, scheduling, budgeting, and implementation. Includes managers in specialized construction fields, such as carpentry or plumbing.

entries.name: Education and Childcare Administrators, Preschool and Daycare
entries.definition: Plan, direct, or coordinate academic or nonacademic activities of preschools or childcare centers and programs, including before- and after-school care. Excludes “Preschool Teachers, Except Special Education” (25-2011) and “Childcare Workers” (39-9011).

entries.name: Education Administrators, Kindergarten through Secondary
entries.definition: Plan, direct, or coordinate the academic, administrative, or auxiliary activities of kindergarten, elementary, or secondary schools.

entries.name: Education Administrators, Postsecondary
entries.definition: Plan, direct, or coordinate student instruction, administration, and services, as well as other research and educational activities, at postsecondary institutions, including universities, colleges, and junior and community colleges.

entries.name: Education Administrators, All Other
entries.definition: All education administrators not listed separately.

entries.name: Architectural and Engineering Managers
entries.definition: Plan, direct, or coordinate activities in such fields as architecture and engineering or research and development in these fields. Excludes “Natural Sciences Managers” (11-9121).

entries.name: Food Service Managers
entries.definition: Plan, direct, or coordinate activities of an organization or department that serves food and beverages. Excludes “Chefs and Head Cooks” (35-1011).

entries.name: Gambling Managers
entries.definition: Plan, direct, or coordinate gambling operations in a casino. May formulate house rules.

entries.name: Entertainment and Recreation Managers, Except Gambling
entries.definition: Plan, direct, or coordinate entertainment and recreational activities and operations of a recreational facility, including cruise ships and parks.

entries.name: Lodging Managers
entries.definition: Plan, direct, or coordinate activities of an organization or department that provides lodging and other accommodations. Excludes “Food Service Managers” (11-9051) in lodging establishments.

entries.name: Medical and Health Services Managers
entries.definition: Plan, direct, or coordinate medical and health services in hospitals, clinics, managed care organizations, public health agencies, or similar organizations.

entries.name: Natural Sciences Managers
entries.definition: Plan, direct, or coordinate activities in such fields as life sciences, physical sciences, mathematics, statistics, and research and development in these fields. Excludes “Computer and Information Systems Managers” (11-3021) and “Architecture and Engineering Managers” (11-9041).

entries.name: Postmasters and Mail Superintendents
entries.definition: Plan, direct, or coordinate operational, administrative, management, and support services of a U.S. post office; or coordinate activities of workers engaged in postal and related work in assigned post office.

entries.name: Property, Real Estate, and Community Association Managers
Property, Real Estate, and Community Association Managers
entries.definition: Plan, direct, or coordinate the selling, buying, leasing, or governance activities of commercial, industrial, or residential real estate properties. Includes managers of homeowner and condominium associations, rented or leased housing units, buildings, or land (including rights-of-way).

entries.name: Social and Community Service Managers
entries.definition: Plan, direct, or coordinate the activities of a social service program or community outreach organization. Oversee the program or organization’s budget and policies regarding participant involvement, program requirements, and benefits. Work may involve directing social workers, counselors, or probation officers.

entries.name: Emergency Management Directors
entries.definition: Plan and direct disaster response or crisis management activities, provide disaster preparedness training, and prepare emergency plans and procedures for natural (e.g., hurricanes, floods, earthquakes), wartime, or technological (e.g., nuclear power plant emergencies or hazardous materials spills) disasters or hostage situations.

entries.name: Funeral Home Managers
entries.definition: Plan, direct, or coordinate the services or resources of funeral homes. Includes activities such as determining prices for services or merchandise and managing the facilities of funeral homes. Excludes “Morticians, Undertakers, and Funeral Arrangers” (39-4031).

entries.name: Personal Service Managers, All Other
entries.definition: All personal service managers not listed separately. Excludes “Financial Specialists” (13-2000). Daycare Managers are included in Education and Childcare Administrators, Preschool and Daycare (11-9031).

entries.name: Managers, All Other
entries.definition: All managers not listed separately.

sections.title: What distinguishes this occupational family
paragraphs: Management Occupations (SOC 11-0000) is a broad occupational major group, not an executive-title directory. It includes top executives, operations specialties managers, managers in functions such as advertising, sales, and human resources, and other management occupations. The structure is useful for consistent occupational coding, but it does not impose a company-wide hierarchy or determine how a particular employer uses titles such as director, vice president, chief officer, or general manager.

Senior roles within the major group can vary in their authority and breadth. One role may lead a whole organization; another may own a specialized function; another may coordinate a multi-location operation. To assess fit, compare the actual work: decisions made, resources controlled, teams led, reporting relationships, and accountability for outcomes. The SOC code helps name the occupational family, while the employer's description and the candidate's evidence establish the particular remit.

A credible management career story shows progression in responsibility rather than relying on title sequence. Explain what changed as the scope grew: the size and composition of teams, budget or operating responsibility, complexity of stakeholders, level of governance, and degree of independent decision-making. Where a role was advisory or project-based rather than line management, say so directly. Accurate distinctions make experience easier to compare and avoid overstating people or operational responsibility.

Transitions between functional management roles are strongest when the candidate can show both transferable leadership practice and relevant domain knowledge. A general manager moving into a specialized function may need evidence of functional judgment; a specialist manager moving toward an enterprise role may need examples of broader integration, trade-offs, and executive governance. The detailed SOC definitions in this page can help identify adjacent occupational concepts, but a code match alone is not a qualification or selection decision.

Search preparation should begin with mandate and environment. Candidates can ask what the role is expected to change, which decisions it owns, how performance is evaluated, and where authority sits relative to the board, CEO, or functional leaders. Confidentiality is important when describing sensitive organizational changes. Use only verifiable evidence, distinguish individual contributions from team outcomes, and do not claim a reporting line or level of authority that the role did not have.

Management is a mode of work rather than a single level in every employer's structure. Some managers direct people and budgets; others manage projects, programs, or a functional specialty. A senior title may involve strategy and governance without direct reports, while a general manager may carry extensive operational responsibility. The SOC definitions provide occupational distinctions, but they do not impose a universal career ladder. Compare duties and the organizational context before inferring equivalence.

When preparing for a senior transition, build an evidence inventory around decisions and scope. Record the teams and functions involved, the decisions made independently, the decisions escalated, the resources controlled, and the outcomes that can be supported. Separate formal authority from influence, and indicate whether a result was achieved personally or collectively. This makes the difference between enterprise leadership, functional leadership, and project contribution clear without inflating a title.

Confidential searches for senior management roles can require careful communication about current employers, board relationships, and succession plans. Establish exclusions and approval boundaries before outreach. A candidate should not imply that an employer has approved a transition or disclose sensitive organizational plans. The right process preserves the candidate's control of disclosures while keeping the career narrative specific enough for a potential employer to assess.

Use the table of official definitions as a vocabulary aid, then return to the employer's actual duties. A carefully explained scope is more useful than claiming a code or title that implies authority the candidate did not hold.

paragraphs: A move from regional managing director to COO depends on whether the target role owns enterprise operations, coordinates functions under a CEO, or leads a defined business area.

The candidate would compare the official SOC hierarchy with the target job's duties, then prepare evidence about decision authority, teams, operating scale, board interaction, and results. Before proceeding, they would clarify what the CEO retains, which functions report to the COO, and how success is measured. This avoids treating similar titles as interchangeable.

sections.title: What distinguishes this occupational family
paragraphs: Legal Occupations (SOC 23-0000) includes lawyers and judges, legal support occupations, and other roles identified in the 2018 SOC structure. It is an occupational classification, not a statement that every person in the group is authorized to practice law in every jurisdiction. The detailed definitions clarify the work category; professional admission, licensing, and permitted scope must be confirmed with the relevant regulator and employer.

Senior legal roles can be organized around advice, transactions, disputes, governance, compliance, public service, or legal operations. The title General Counsel is not itself a SOC code and can carry different authority across employers. A candidate's experience should clarify whether they advised, decided, managed external counsel, led a department, appeared in court, negotiated transactions, or held a formal officer role. Those distinctions help employers understand both capability and limits.

A legal executive's leadership story should make the jurisdiction, subject matter, and organizational context legible without revealing privileged or confidential information. Describe the kinds of matters handled at a high level, the decision process, the stakeholder relationships, and the governance contribution. Do not disclose client identity or sensitive legal advice. Where outcomes were shared with a team, describe the individual responsibility precisely rather than claiming a result on behalf of the whole organization.

Transitions can cross private practice, in-house work, government, and legal-support functions, but they involve distinct duties and qualification requirements. A strong move rationale identifies transferable judgment and stakeholder skills while addressing the new role's jurisdiction, admission, subject-matter, or public-service requirements. SOC's hierarchy can aid comparison, but does not certify equivalence, professional standing, or eligibility to practice.

For a cross-border search, verify where the work will be performed, which entity the role supports, the governing jurisdiction, and whether admission or another authorization is required. Titles, professional qualifications, and reserved activities differ between countries. Use official professional bodies or regulators and qualified legal advisers for those questions. KOV's role is candidate-side career support and positioning, not legal advice or recruitment on behalf of an employer.

Legal leadership combines professional judgment with organizational governance, but the balance differs by employer. Some general counsel roles are focused on advice and risk; others include company-secretary, compliance, government-relations, or broader executive duties. A job title does not establish board membership, officer status, or authority over every legal matter. Candidates should define the reporting relationship, decision rights, jurisdictions served, and use of external counsel, then compare that scope with the target position.

The distinction between practicing law and leading a legal operation is important in cross-functional or international transitions. A legal operations leader may manage systems, budgets, outside counsel, and service design without holding the same professional duties as an admitted lawyer. Conversely, an experienced lawyer may need to demonstrate team leadership and commercial judgment for an executive role. The SOC hierarchy identifies occupational categories but does not determine admission or reserved activities.

Interview examples should protect privilege and confidentiality. Candidates can explain the nature of a challenge, their process for assessing risk, how they advised decision-makers, and the general outcome without naming parties or revealing legal advice. If an example cannot be discussed safely, choose another. For any uncertainty about disclosure obligations, professional duties, or admission, consult a qualified lawyer or regulator rather than treating career guidance as legal advice.

Classification must remain separate from professional status. SOC describes occupational work; it does not grant admission, verify good standing, authorize cross-border practice, or replace the rules of a court, bar, law society, or regulator. A precise account of jurisdiction and responsibility helps prevent readers from inferring a qualification that has not been established. Candidates should make those limits clear in public profiles and private discussions.

Agents and Business Managers of Artists, Performers, and Athletes
entries.definition: Represent and promote artists, performers, and athletes in dealings with current or prospective employers. May handle contract negotiation and other business matters for clients.

entries.name: Buyers and Purchasing Agents, Farm Products
entries.definition: Purchase farm products either for further processing or resale. Includes tree farm contractors, grain brokers and market operators, grain buyers, and tobacco buyers. May negotiate contracts.

entries.name: Wholesale and Retail Buyers, Except Farm Products
entries.definition: Buy merchandise or commodities, other than farm products, for resale to consumers at the wholesale or retail level, including both durable and nondurable goods. Analyze past buying trends, sales records, price, and quality of merchandise to determine value and yield. Select, order, and authorize payment for merchandise according to contractual agreements. May conduct meetings with sales personnel and introduce new products. May negotiate contracts. Includes assistant wholesale and retail buyers of nonfarm products. Claims Adjusters, Examiners, and Investigators
entries.definition: Review settled claims to determine that payments and settlements are made in accordance with company practices and procedures. Confer with legal counsel on claims requiring litigation. May also settle insurance claims. Excludes “Fire Inspectors and Investigators” (33-2021).

entries.name: Insurance Appraisers, Auto Damage
entries.definition: Appraise automobile or other vehicle damage to determine repair costs for insurance claim settlement. Prepare insurance forms to indicate repair cost or cost estimates and recommendations. May seek agreement with automotive repair shop on repair costs.

entries.name: Compliance Officers
entries.definition: Examine, evaluate, and investigate eligibility for or conformity with laws and regulations governing contract compliance of licenses and permits, and perform other compliance and enforcement inspection and analysis activities not classified elsewhere. Excludes “Financial Examiners" (13-2061), “Tax Examiners and Collectors, and Revenue Agents” (13-2081), “Occupational Health and Safety Specialists” (19-5011), “Occupational Health and Safety Technicians” (19-5012), “Transportation Security Screeners” (33-9093), “Agricultural Inspectors” (45-2011), “Construction and Building Inspectors” (47-4011), and “Transportation Inspectors” (53-6051).

entries.name: Cost Estimators
entries.definition: Prepare cost estimates for product manufacturing, construction projects, or services to aid management in bidding on or determining price of product or service. May specialize according to particular service performed or type of product manufactured.

entries.name: Human Resources Specialists
entries.definition: Recruit, screen, interview, or place individuals within an organization. May perform other activities in multiple human resources areas. Excludes “Compensation, Benefits, and Job Analysis Specialists” (13-1141) and “Training and Development Specialists” (13-1151).

entries.name: Farm Labor Contractors
entries.definition: Recruit and hire seasonal or temporary agricultural laborers. May transport, house, and provide meals for workers.

entries.name: Labor Relations Specialists
entries.definition: Resolve disputes between workers and managers, negotiate collective bargaining agreements, or coordinate grievance procedures to handle employee complaints. Excludes equal employment opportunity (EEO) officers, who are included in “Compliance Officers” (13-1041).

entries.name: Logisticians
entries.definition: Analyze and coordinate the ongoing logistical functions of a firm or organization. Responsible for the entire life cycle of a product, including acquisition, distribution, internal allocation, delivery, and final disposal of resources. Excludes “Transportation, Storage, and Distribution Managers” (11-3071) and “Project Management Specialists” (13-1082).

entries.name: Project Management Specialists
entries.definition: Analyze and coordinate the schedule, timeline, procurement, staffing, and budget of a product or service on a per project basis. Lead and guide the work of technical staff. May serve as a point of contact for the client or customer. Excludes “Management Occupations” (11-0000), “Logisticians” (13-1081), “Meeting, Convention, and Event Planners” (13-1121), and “Production, Planning, and Expediting Clerks” (43-5061).

entries.name: Management Analysts
entries.definition: Conduct organizational studies and evaluations, design systems and procedures, conduct work simplification and measurement studies, and prepare operations and procedures manuals to assist management in operating more efficiently and effectively. Includes program analysts and management consultants. Excludes “Computer Systems Analysts” (15-1211) and “Operations Research Analysts” (15-2031).

entries.name: Meeting, Convention, and Event Planners
entries.definition: Coordinate activities of staff, convention personnel, or clients to make arrangements for group meetings, events, or conventions.

entries.name: Fundraisers
entries.definition: Organize activities to raise funds or otherwise solicit and gather monetary donations or other gifts for an organization. May design and produce promotional materials. May also raise awareness of the organization’s work, goals, and financial needs.

entries.name: Compensation, Benefits, and Job Analysis Specialists
Compensation, Benefits, and Job Analysis Specialists
entries.definition: Conduct programs of compensation and benefits and job analysis for employer. May specialize in specific areas, such as position classification and pension programs.

entries.name: Training and Development Specialists
entries.definition: Design or conduct work-related training and development programs to improve individual skills or organizational performance. May analyze organizational training needs or evaluate training effectiveness. Excludes “Career/Technical Education Teachers, Postsecondary” (25-1194) and “Other Teachers and Instructors” (25-3000). Flight instructors are included with “Aircraft Pilots and Flight Engineers” (53-2010).

entries.name: Market Research Analysts and Marketing Specialists
Market Research Analysts and Marketing Specialists
entries.definition: Research conditions in local, regional, national, or online markets. Gather information to determine potential sales of a product or service, or plan a marketing or advertising campaign. May gather information on competitors, prices, sales, and methods of marketing and distribution. May employ search marketing tactics, analyze web metrics, and develop recommendations to increase search engine ranking and visibility to target markets. Excludes “Web and Digital Interface Designers” (15-1255), “Art Directors” (27-1011), “Graphic Designers” (27-1024), and “Public Relations Specialists” (27-3031).

entries.name: Business Operations Specialists, All Other
entries.definition: All business operations specialists not listed separately.

entries.name: Accountants and Auditors
entries.definition: Examine, analyze, and interpret accounting records to prepare financial statements, give advice, or audit and evaluate statements prepared by others. Install or advise on systems of recording costs or other financial and budgetary data. Excludes “Tax Examiners and Collectors, and Revenue Agents” (13-2081).

entries.name: Appraisers of Personal and Business Property
entries.definition: Appraise and estimate the fair value of tangible personal or business property, such as jewelry, art, antiques, collectibles, and equipment. Includes workers who appraise both personal and business property as well as real estate. May also appraise land. Excludes “Claims Adjusters, Examiners, and Investigators” (13-1031), “Insurance Appraisers, Auto Damage” (13-1032), “Appraisers and Assessors of Real Estate” (13-2023), and “Tax Examiners and Collectors, and Revenue Agents” (13-2081).

entries.name: Appraisers and Assessors of Real Estate
entries.definition: Appraise real estate, exclusively, and estimate its fair value. May assess taxes in accordance with prescribed schedules. Excludes “Appraisers of Personal and Business Property” (13-2022).

entries.name: Budget Analysts
entries.definition: Examine budget estimates for completeness, accuracy, and conformance with procedures and regulations. Analyze budgeting and accounting reports. Excludes “Financial and Investment Analysts” (13-2051).

entries.name: Credit Analysts
entries.definition: Analyze credit data and financial statements of individuals or firms to determine the degree of risk involved in extending credit or lending money. Prepare reports with credit information for use in decisionmaking. Excludes “Financial Risk Specialists” (13-2054).

entries.name: Financial and Investment Analysts
entries.definition: Conduct quantitative analyses of information involving investment programs or financial data of public or private institutions, including valuation of businesses. Excludes “Budget Analysts” (13-2031), “Financial Risk Specialists” (13-2054), and “Securities, Commodities, and Financial Services Sales Agents” (41-3031).

entries.name: Personal Financial Advisors
entries.definition: Advise clients on financial plans using knowledge of tax and investment strategies, securities, insurance, pension plans, and real estate. Duties include assessing clients' assets, liabilities, cash flow, insurance coverage, tax status, and financial objectives. May also buy and sell financial assets for clients. Excludes “Securities, Commodities, and Financial Services Sales Agents” (41-3031).

entries.name: Insurance Underwriters
entries.definition: Review individual applications for insurance to evaluate degree of risk involved and determine acceptance of applications.

entries.name: Financial Risk Specialists
entries.definition: Analyze and measure exposure to credit and market risk threatening the assets, earning capacity, or economic state of an organization. May make recommendations to limit risk. Excludes “Credit Analysts” (13-2041).

entries.name: Financial Examiners
entries.definition: Enforce or ensure compliance with laws and regulations governing financial and securities institutions and financial and real estate transactions. May examine, verify, or authenticate records.

entries.name: Credit Counselors
entries.definition: Advise and educate individuals or organizations on acquiring and managing debt. May provide guidance in determining the best type of loan and explain loan requirements or restrictions. May help develop debt management plans or student financial aid packages. May advise on credit issues, or provide budget, mortgage, bankruptcy, or student financial aid counseling.

entries.name: Loan Officers
entries.definition: Evaluate, authorize, or recommend approval of commercial, real estate, or credit loans. Advise borrowers on financial status and payment methods. Includes mortgage loan officers and agents, collection analysts, loan servicing officers, loan underwriters, and payday loan officers.

entries.name: Tax Examiners, Collectors and Preparers, and Revenue Agents
Tax Examiners and Collectors, and Revenue Agents
entries.definition: Determine tax liability or collect taxes from individuals or business firms according to prescribed laws and regulations.

entries.name: Tax Preparers
entries.definition: Prepare tax returns for individuals or small businesses. Excludes “Accountants and Auditors” (13-2011).

entries.name: Financial Specialists, All Other
entries.definition: All financial specialists not listed separately.

sections.title: What distinguishes this occupational family
paragraphs: Business and Financial Operations Occupations (SOC 13-0000) spans work such as finance, accounting, analysis, compliance, human resources, project management, procurement, and related organizational functions. The 2018 classification provides a structured way to distinguish the work; it does not determine an individual's seniority or how a company organizes its departments. The full hierarchy below allows readers to explore minor, broad, and detailed occupational concepts using official codes and definitions.

Senior leaders in these functions commonly need to translate specialist knowledge into decisions that other executives can use. A finance leader may explain financial performance and trade-offs; a risk or compliance leader may clarify exposure and controls; an HR executive may align workforce strategy and operating needs; a procurement or project leader may coordinate resources and delivery. These examples are functional lenses, not a claim that every role carries the same duties.

The strongest career evidence makes the scale and decision context visible. Describe what information or process you owned, who relied on it, how your analysis informed action, and which outcomes can be attributed to your work. For controls, compliance, finance, or people matters, maintain confidentiality and avoid implying that a process had a regulatory outcome unless that is documented and within your remit. Distinguish line leadership from advisory, specialist, and project contributions.

Transitions between specialties are possible when the candidate can explain the bridge. A finance transformation leader moving toward enterprise operations should show cross-functional delivery and governance, not only system implementation. A compliance leader moving into broader risk leadership should demonstrate the risk domains and committee relationships actually covered. A project leader moving into a permanent business role should explain sustained accountability beyond a temporary initiative.

The SOC labels can help a candidate choose clear language, but they should not be treated as job descriptions. Employers combine and rename functions, and a single title may cover different work in different organizations. Compare the target responsibilities, reporting relationships, systems, stakeholders, and measures of success. For international roles, verify local requirements and market context with current official sources; this directory itself does not measure employment demand.

The major group includes both analytical specialties and operational disciplines. A senior function may be responsible for interpreting information, setting policies, managing controls, or executing services. These are distinct contributions even where the same employer combines them under one department. Candidates should identify the main decisions the role enables, who owns the resulting action, and whether the candidate advises, approves, or operates the process.

Enterprise leadership in finance, human resources, compliance, procurement, and project delivery often depends on influence across functions. Evidence should describe how the candidate aligned stakeholders, handled competing priorities, and established accountability. Where data or measurement was used, define the baseline and period. Avoid implying a causal outcome when many teams or external conditions contributed. The detailed SOC definitions can help frame the occupational language, but an employer's specific remit remains decisive.

Some transitions move from a specialist role into a broader executive remit. That step usually requires evidence beyond technical knowledge: resource decisions, governance, communication with senior stakeholders, team leadership, and responsibility after a recommendation was made. Candidates can use examples of sustained ownership, not only one-off projects, to show readiness. If a target role adds regulated, professional, or jurisdiction-specific responsibilities, identify those requirements early and verify them independently.

The definitions are reference material, not a substitute for the target employer's job description. Use both to identify overlap and difference, then support the candidate's fit with examples that can be verified and safely disclosed. Explain the decision context and where accountability sat, especially when functions were shared among several leaders. Be specific about the actual contribution.

The candidate would map the target remit against the SOC definitions and the employer's job description, then separate transformation achievements from recurring operational ownership. They would prepare evidence of stakeholder decisions, controls, adoption, and outcomes, while identifying areas where the new sector's requirements need further research.

Depending on the engagement, support may help define a target, organize evidence, research organizations, and coordinate approved applications or outreach. The professional remains the decision-maker, and employers control selection.

SOC is a reference for work performed, not proof of a candidate's qualifications or a promise of access to a role. Scope, deliverables, approvals, and fees are agreed in writing before work begins. No interview, offer, or employment outcome is guaranteed.

faqs.question: What does SOC 13-0000 cover?
faqs.answer: It is the major group for Business and Financial Operations occupations, with the official hierarchy listed in this directory.

faqs.question: Does the group include only accountants?
faqs.answer: No. It contains several business and financial specialties. Consult the official code and definition for the precise occupation.

faqs.question: How many detailed occupations are included?
faqs.answer: The verified BLS structure and definitions workbooks list 35 detailed occupations under SOC 13-0000.

faqs.question: Can a finance leader move into broader operations?
faqs.answer: Potentially, if they can show sustained operating scope, cross-functional decisions, and outcomes beyond financial analysis.

faqs.question: Are these codes job titles?
faqs.answer: They are occupational classifications, not a guarantee that an employer uses that exact title or combines duties the same way.

faqs.question: Does KOV represent employers hiring these roles?
faqs.answer: No. KOV provides candidate-side services to professionals; employers make their own hiring decisions.
