entries.name: Computer Systems Analysts
entries.definition: Analyze science, engineering, business, and other data processing problems to develop and implement solutions to complex applications problems, system administration issues, or network concerns. Perform systems management and integration functions, improve existing computer systems, and review computer system capabilities, workflow, and schedule limitations. May analyze or recommend commercially available software.

entries.name: Information Security Analysts
entries.definition: Plan, implement, upgrade, or monitor security measures for the protection of computer networks and information. Assess system vulnerabilities for security risks and propose and implement risk mitigation strategies. May ensure appropriate security controls are in place that will safeguard digital files and vital electronic infrastructure. May respond to computer security breaches and viruses. Excludes “Computer Network Architects” (15-1241).

entries.name: Computer and Information Research Scientists
entries.definition: Conduct research into fundamental computer and information science as theorists, designers, or inventors. Develop solutions to problems in the field of computer hardware and software.

entries.name: Computer Network Support Specialists
entries.definition: Analyze, test, troubleshoot, and evaluate existing network systems, such as local area networks (LAN), wide area networks (WAN), cloud networks, servers, and other data communications networks. Perform network maintenance to ensure networks operate correctly with minimal interruption. Excludes “Computer Network Architects” (15-1241) and “Network and Computer Systems Administrators” (15-1244).

entries.name: Computer User Support Specialists
entries.definition: Provide technical assistance to computer users. Answer questions or resolve computer problems for clients in person, via telephone, or electronically. May provide assistance concerning the use of computer hardware and software, including printing, installation, word processing, electronic mail, and operating systems. Excludes “Network and Computer Systems Administrators” (15-1244).

entries.name: Database and Network Administrators and Architects
Computer Network Architects
entries.definition: Design and implement computer and information networks, such as local area networks (LAN), wide area networks (WAN), intranets, extranets, and other data communications networks. Perform network modeling, analysis, and planning, including analysis of capacity needs for network infrastructures. May also design network and computer security measures. May research and recommend network and data communications hardware and software. Excludes “Information Security Analysts” (15-1212), “Computer Network Support Specialists” (15-1231), and “Network and Computer Systems Administrators” (15-1244).

entries.name: Database Administrators
entries.definition: Administer, test, and implement computer databases, applying knowledge of database management systems. Coordinate changes to computer databases. Identify, investigate, and resolve database performance issues, database capacity, and database scalability. May plan, coordinate, and implement security measures to safeguard computer databases. Excludes “Information Security Analysts” (15-1212) and “Database Architects” (15-1243).

entries.name: Database Architects
entries.definition: Design strategies for enterprise databases, data warehouse systems, and multidimensional networks. Set standards for database operations, programming, query processes, and security. Model, design, and construct large relational databases or data warehouses. Create and optimize data models for warehouse infrastructure and workflow. Integrate new systems with existing warehouse structure and refine system performance and functionality. Excludes “Database Administrators” (15-1242).

entries.name: Network and Computer Systems Administrators
entries.definition: Install, configure, and maintain an organization’s local area network (LAN), wide area network (WAN), data communications network, operating systems, and physical and virtual servers. Perform system monitoring and verify the integrity and availability of hardware, network, and server resources and systems. Review system and application logs and verify completion of scheduled jobs, including system backups. Analyze network and server resource consumption and control user access. Install and upgrade software and maintain software licenses. May assist in network modeling, analysis, planning, and coordination between network and data communications hardware and software. Excludes “Information Security Analysts” (15-1212), “Computer Network Support Specialists” (15-1231), and “Computer User Support Specialists” (15-1232).

entries.name: Software and Web Developers, Programmers, and Testers
Computer Programmers
entries.definition: Create, modify, and test the code and scripts that allow computer applications to run. Work from specifications drawn up by software and web developers or other individuals. May develop and write computer programs to store, locate, and retrieve specific documents, data, and information.

entries.name: Software Developers
entries.definition: Research, design, and develop computer and network software or specialized utility programs. Analyze user needs and develop software solutions, applying principles and techniques of computer science, engineering, and mathematical analysis. Update software or enhance existing software capabilities. May work with computer hardware engineers to integrate hardware and software systems, and develop specifications and performance requirements. May maintain databases within an application area, working individually or coordinating database development as part of a team.

entries.name: Software Quality Assurance Analysts and Testers
entries.definition: Develop and execute software tests to identify software problems and their causes. Test system modifications to prepare for implementation. Document software and application defects using a bug tracking system and report defects to software or web developers. Create and maintain databases of known defects. May participate in software design reviews to provide input on functional requirements, operational characteristics, product designs, and schedules.

entries.name: Web Developers
entries.definition: Develop and implement websites, web applications, application databases, and interactive web interfaces. Evaluate code to ensure that it is properly structured, meets industry standards, and is compatible with browsers and devices. Optimize website performance, scalability, and server-side code and processes. May develop website infrastructure and integrate websites with other computer applications. Excludes “Special Effects Artists and Animators” (27-1014).

entries.name: Web and Digital Interface Designers
entries.definition: Design digital user interfaces or websites. Develop and test layouts, interfaces, functionality, and navigation menus to ensure compatibility and usability across browsers or devices. May use web framework applications as well as client-side code and processes. May evaluate web design following web and accessibility standards, and may analyze web use metrics and optimize websites for marketability and search engine ranking. May design and test interfaces that facilitate the human-computer interaction and maximize the usability of digital devices, websites, and software with a focus on aesthetics and design. May create graphics used in websites and manage website content and links. Excludes “Special Effects Artists and Animators” (27-1014) and “Graphic Designers” (27-1024).

entries.name: Computer Occupations, All Other
entries.definition: All computer occupations not listed separately. Excludes “Computer and Information Systems Managers” (11-3021), “Computer Hardware Engineers” (17-2061), “Electrical and Electronics Engineers” (17-2070), “Computer Science Teachers, Postsecondary” (25-1021), “Special Effects Artists and Animators” (27-1014), “Graphic Designers” (27-1024), “Health Information Technologists and Medical Registrars” (29-9021), and “Computer, Automated Teller, and Office Machine Repairers” (49-2011).

entries.name: Actuaries
entries.definition: Analyze statistical data, such as mortality, accident, sickness, disability, and retirement rates and construct probability tables to forecast risk and liability for payment of future benefits. May ascertain insurance rates required and cash reserves necessary to ensure payment of future benefits.

entries.name: Mathematicians
entries.definition: Conduct research in fundamental mathematics or in application of mathematical techniques to science, management, and other fields. Solve problems in various fields using mathematical methods.

entries.name: Operations Research Analysts
entries.definition: Formulate and apply mathematical modeling and other optimizing methods to develop and interpret information that assists management with decisionmaking, policy formulation, or other managerial functions. May collect and analyze data and develop decision support software, services, or products. May develop and supply optimal time, cost, or logistics networks for program evaluation, review, or implementation.

entries.name: Statisticians
entries.definition: Develop or apply mathematical or statistical theory and methods to collect, organize, interpret, and summarize numerical data to provide usable information. May specialize in fields such as biostatistics, agricultural statistics, business statistics, or economic statistics. Includes mathematical and survey statisticians. Excludes “Survey Researchers” (19-3022).

entries.name: Data Scientists
entries.definition: Develop and implement a set of techniques or analytics applications to transform raw data into meaningful information using data-oriented programming languages and visualization software. Apply data mining, data modeling, natural language processing, and machine learning to extract and analyze information from large structured and unstructured datasets. Visualize, interpret, and report data findings. May create dynamic data reports. Excludes “Statisticians” (15-2041), “Cartographers and Photogrammetrists” (17-1021), and “Health Information Technologists and Medical Registrars” (29-9021).

entries.name: Mathematical Science Occupations, All Other
entries.definition: All mathematical scientists not listed separately.

sections.title: What distinguishes this occupational family
paragraphs: Computer and Mathematical Occupations (SOC 15-0000) includes computer and information research, software development, data and mathematical work, systems analysis, security, network and systems administration, and related technical occupations. The official hierarchy separates occupational concepts by work performed, not by technology brand, employer industry, or seniority. A code cannot tell a reader whether a role is an individual contributor, a people manager, or an executive; the specific responsibilities and reporting relationships must be examined.

Senior technology titles are particularly variable. A CTO may lead product engineering, enterprise technology, research, security, or a combination; a CIO may focus on internal systems or data; a chief data officer may hold governance, analytics, or platform responsibilities. Those titles are not SOC categories by themselves. Candidates should specify whether they owned architecture, delivery, reliability, security, product direction, internal platforms, or technical strategy, and show how their authority related to the rest of the organization.

Strong technical leadership evidence connects technical decisions with organizational context. Describe the problem, constraints, architecture or method at a level that can be shared, the teams and stakeholders involved, and the trade-offs made. Explain reliability, security, data quality, customer, or cost outcomes only when the evidence is accurate and disclosable. Avoid describing a team result as an individual achievement or claiming broad transformation without stating what was actually changed.

Career transitions across technical specialties depend on scope and fundamentals. A software leader moving toward data infrastructure may need evidence of platform reliability and governance; a security executive moving into enterprise technology should explain broader operating responsibilities; a researcher moving into product leadership should show how research translated into a roadmap or user outcome. The detailed definitions can guide role comparisons, while the target employer's systems, scale, and risk profile determine the actual fit.

International role research should distinguish a global remit from local employment and authority. Confirm the legal entity, reporting line, customer or internal user base, security obligations, and expected operating hours or location. Requirements and labor-market conditions change; use current official sources for each market and avoid treating the SOC hierarchy as a forecast. This page is a classification resource and candidate-career guide, not a technical audit or hiring-demand report.

Technical occupations span research, software, systems, security, data, networks, and mathematical work. The detailed SOC hierarchy distinguishes these types of work but does not encode architecture choices, programming languages, operating scale, or management level. A career profile should therefore connect the code to the work: systems built or governed, users served, risk handled, team structure, and the decisions for which the candidate was accountable.

Executive technology roles also differ in how close they are to product delivery, enterprise IT, infrastructure, data, or security governance. A candidate should describe the technical and organizational boundary of their remit and how it related to peers in product, operations, finance, risk, and commercial functions. State what you directly owned and what you influenced. This avoids a common mismatch in which one executive title is assumed to carry the same technical authority across organizations.

Security, privacy, and resilience examples can be sensitive. Discuss the governance, decision process, and high-level result without exposing exploitable system detail, confidential incidents, or proprietary architecture. If a metric is used, explain the scope and period without suggesting a guarantee of future performance. For an international search, confirm the target's regulatory and operational expectations with current official sources and the employer, rather than relying on a general SOC label.

Treat the SOC definition as an occupational reference, not as a technical specification. Validate the target's actual platform, team, scale, and accountability before equating two roles or presenting an experience match.

Chief information officer

Describe enterprise systems, service delivery, data, resilience, and governance scope.
Chief information security officer

Chief data or analytics executive

Distinguish data stewardship from analytics delivery and describe the authority held.
Engineering or product executive
Leads technical teams and product or engineering delivery in the employer's operating model.
Show product lifecycle, team scale, delivery practices, and measurable customer or business evidence.

sections.title: Compare the role's actual duties
paragraphs: A move from enterprise CIO in manufacturing to CTO in a software company may require direct product-engineering and customer-platform leadership in addition to large-scale systems, security governance, and vendor management.

Preparation would compare the detailed SOC concepts with the job's actual responsibilities, map the candidate's technical and executive evidence, and identify gaps in product ownership or engineering delivery. The candidate would ask how architecture decisions are made, who owns security and reliability, and what the CTO can decide independently.

sections.title: How Construction is classified and led
paragraphs: The 2022 NAICS classification places Construction in sector 23. Its subsector structure includes Construction of Buildings, Heavy and Civil Engineering Construction, Specialty Trade Contractors. Those official labels are useful for identifying the establishment activity a classification describes; they are not a measure of company size, prestige, hiring demand, or a candidate's occupational specialty. Begin with the business activity shown in the source table, then confirm that it matches the actual entity and operations under consideration.

Inside this sector, the industry-group level includes Residential Building Construction, Nonresidential Building Construction, Utility System Construction, Land Subdivision, Highway, Street, and Bridge Construction. That range of labels gives a more precise starting point than using the sector name alone. For a senior search, compare the employer's products or services, customers, revenue model, operating footprint, ownership, and governance with the specific activity represented by its code. The classification does not describe an executive's remit, so verify accountability through the job description, reporting line, decision rights, and employer disclosures rather than inferring them from NAICS.

Leadership work should be evaluated through decisions and evidence. A finance leader may need to explain planning, reporting, capital, or stewardship responsibilities; an operations leader may need to establish the service, production, delivery, or control scope they owned. These are questions to investigate, not assumptions about every employer in the sector. Candidates should distinguish their own contribution from team results, define the period and scale of any figures they share, and avoid disclosing confidential commercial, employee, customer, or transaction information.

Transitions within Construction can involve materially different operating contexts even when the businesses sit in one sector. Compare the subsector names—such as Construction of Buildings, Heavy and Civil Engineering Construction, Specialty Trade Contractors—with the target organization's activity and the role's actual mandate. A transferable capability is strongest when the candidate can show how it was applied, which stakeholders were affected, and what responsibility they held. Where the target requires a credential, regulated approval, technical background, or local experience, confirm the requirement through the employer and relevant official authority.

The directory reports 28 five-digit industries and 31 six-digit U.S. national industries beneath this sector. These are distinct levels in the official structure; the U.S. national detail should not be collapsed into or substituted for the five-digit count. Parent codes make the relationships auditable and the source marker T, where displayed, records the workbook's trilateral-agreement indicator. Use the code table as a research map, not as a ranking of employers or a forecast of market conditions.

For a location comparison, first define the target job and employing entity, then check the organization's activity, operating geography, role requirements, work authorization, and decision authority. The United States, Canada, United Kingdom, UAE, Saudi Arabia, and Australia do not share one industry classification or one set of employment rules. Current market facts must be verified against dated employer disclosures and official sources. This guide does not claim current vacancies, compensation levels, regulatory status, or relative demand.

sections.title: How Wholesale Trade is classified and led
paragraphs: The 2022 NAICS classification places Wholesale Trade in sector 42. Its subsector structure includes Merchant Wholesalers, Durable Goods, Merchant Wholesalers, Nondurable Goods, Wholesale Trade Agents and Brokers. Those official labels are useful for identifying the establishment activity a classification describes; they are not a measure of company size, prestige, hiring demand, or a candidate's occupational specialty. Begin with the business activity shown in the source table, then confirm that it matches the actual entity and operations under consideration.

Inside this sector, the industry-group level includes Motor Vehicle and Motor Vehicle Parts and Supplies Merchant Wholesalers, Furniture and Home Furnishing Merchant Wholesalers, Lumber and Other Construction Materials Merchant Wholesalers, Professional and Commercial Equipment and Supplies Merchant Wholesalers, Metal and Mineral (except Petroleum) Merchant Wholesalers. That range of labels gives a more precise starting point than using the sector name alone. For a senior search, compare the employer's products or services, customers, revenue model, operating footprint, ownership, and governance with the specific activity represented by its code. The classification does not describe an executive's remit, so verify accountability through the job description, reporting line, decision rights, and employer disclosures rather than inferring them from NAICS.

Leadership work should be evaluated through decisions and evidence. A finance leader may need to explain planning, reporting, capital, or stewardship responsibilities; an operations leader may need to establish the service, production, delivery, or control scope they owned. These are questions to investigate, not assumptions about every employer in the sector. Candidates should distinguish their own contribution from team results, define the period and scale of any figures they share, and avoid disclosing confidential commercial, employee, customer, or transaction information.

Transitions within Wholesale Trade can involve materially different operating contexts even when the businesses sit in one sector. Compare the subsector names—such as Merchant Wholesalers, Durable Goods, Merchant Wholesalers, Nondurable Goods, Wholesale Trade Agents and Brokers—with the target organization's activity and the role's actual mandate. Use the code table as a research map, not as a ranking of employers or a forecast of market conditions.

sections.title: How Transportation and Warehousing is classified and led
paragraphs: The 2022 NAICS classification places Transportation and Warehousing in sector 48-49. Its subsector structure includes Air Transportation, Rail Transportation, Water Transportation, Truck Transportation, Transit and Ground Passenger Transportation. Those official labels are useful for identifying the establishment activity a classification describes; they are not a measure of company size, prestige, hiring demand, or a candidate's occupational specialty. Begin with the business activity shown in the source table, then confirm that it matches the actual entity and operations under consideration.

Inside this sector, the industry-group level includes Scheduled Air Transportation, Nonscheduled Air Transportation, Rail Transportation, Deep Sea, Coastal, and Great Lakes Water Transportation, Inland Water Transportation. That range of labels gives a more precise starting point than using the sector name alone. For a senior search, compare the employer's products or services, customers, revenue model, operating footprint, ownership, and governance with the specific activity represented by its code. The classification does not describe an executive's remit, so verify accountability through the job description, reporting line, decision rights, and employer disclosures rather than inferring them from NAICS.

Leadership work should be evaluated through decisions and evidence. A finance leader may need to explain planning, reporting, capital, or stewardship responsibilities; an operations leader may need to establish the service, production, delivery, or control scope they owned. These are questions to investigate, not assumptions about every employer in the sector. Candidates should distinguish their own contribution from team results, define the period and scale of any figures they share, and avoid disclosing confidential commercial, employee, customer, or transaction information.

Transitions within Transportation and Warehousing can involve materially different operating contexts even when the businesses sit in one sector. Compare the subsector names—such as Air Transportation, Rail Transportation, Water Transportation, Truck Transportation, Transit and Ground Passenger Transportation—with the target organization's activity and the role's actual mandate. A transferable capability is strongest when the candidate can show how it was applied, which stakeholders were affected, and what responsibility they held. Where the target requires a credential, regulated approval, technical background, or local experience, confirm the requirement through the employer and relevant official authority.

Parent codes make the relationships auditable and the source marker T, where displayed, records the workbook's trilateral-agreement indicator. Use the code table as a research map, not as a ranking of employers or a forecast of market conditions.

sections.title: How Public Administration is classified and led
paragraphs: The 2022 NAICS classification places Public Administration in sector 92. Its subsector structure includes Executive, Legislative, and Other General Government Support, Justice, Public Order, and Safety Activities, Administration of Human Resource Programs, Administration of Environmental Quality Programs, Administration of Housing Programs, Urban Planning, and Community Development. Those official labels are useful for identifying the establishment activity a classification describes; they are not a measure of company size, prestige, hiring demand, or a candidate's occupational specialty. Begin with the business activity shown in the source table, then confirm that it matches the actual entity and operations under consideration.

Inside this sector, the industry-group level includes Executive, Legislative, and Other General Government Support, Justice, Public Order, and Safety Activities, Administration of Human Resource Programs, Administration of Environmental Quality Programs, Administration of Housing Programs, Urban Planning, and Community Development. That range of labels gives a more precise starting point than using the sector name alone. For a senior search, compare the employer's products or services, customers, revenue model, operating footprint, ownership, and governance with the specific activity represented by its code. The classification does not describe an executive's remit, so verify accountability through the job description, reporting line, decision rights, and employer disclosures rather than inferring them from NAICS.

Leadership work should be evaluated through decisions and evidence. A finance leader may need to explain planning, reporting, capital, or stewardship responsibilities; an operations leader may need to establish the service, production, delivery, or control scope they owned. These are questions to investigate, not assumptions about every employer in the sector. Candidates should distinguish their own contribution from team results, define the period and scale of any figures they share, and avoid disclosing confidential commercial, employee, customer, or transaction information.

Transitions within Public Administration can involve materially different operating contexts even when the businesses sit in one sector. Compare the subsector names—such as Executive, Legislative, and Other General Government Support, Justice, Public Order, and Safety Activities, Administration of Human Resource Programs, Administration of Environmental Quality Programs, Administration of Housing Programs, Urban Planning, and Community Development—with the target organization's activity and the role's actual mandate. A transferable capability is strongest when the candidate can show how it was applied, which stakeholders were affected, and what responsibility they held. Where the target requires a credential, regulated approval, technical background, or local experience, confirm the requirement through the employer and relevant official authority.

The directory reports 29 five-digit industries and 29 six-digit U.S. national industries beneath this sector. These are distinct levels in the official structure; the U.S. national detail should not be collapsed into or substituted for the five-digit count. Parent codes make the relationships auditable and the source marker T, where displayed, records the workbook's trilateral-agreement indicator. Use the code table as a research map, not as a ranking of employers or a forecast of market conditions.

For a location comparison, first define the target job and employing entity, then check the organization's activity, operating geography, role requirements, work authorization, and decision authority. The United States, Canada, United Kingdom, UAE, Saudi Arabia, and Australia do not share one industry classification or one set of employment rules. Current market facts must be verified against dated employer disclosures and official sources. This guide does not claim current vacancies, compensation levels, regulatory status, or relative demand.

KOV Career Agency provides candidate-side career representation and individual career services. Depending on the written engagement, support can include defining target organizations, researching role context, positioning verified experience, and coordinating applications or outreach approved by the professional. The candidate retains approval of external activity, and employers retain hiring decisions. Scope, deliverables, fees, and reporting are agreed before work begins; no interview, offer, job, or timeline is guaranteed.

For a practical Public Administration search, keep a short evidence file linking each target organization to its verified activity, the role's stated remit, and the experience that supports your fit. Record open questions separately from confirmed facts. This helps prevent a broad sector label from substituting for due diligence and makes conversations more specific without exposing confidential employer information.

Use the hierarchy for sector 92 as a set of progressively more specific questions. First confirm the establishment's primary activity; then check whether a subsidiary, business unit, or separate location has a different classification. Next compare that activity with the role's stated scope and the organization's own public descriptions. A code can support a consistent research note, but it cannot replace due diligence on ownership, customers, services, operating model, or the accountability attached to a particular executive position.

directory.sourceName: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2018 SOC
directory.sourceNote: Source files: data/taxonomy/soc_structure_2018.xlsx and data/taxonomy/soc_2018_definitions.xlsx. Definitions are official BLS text; SOC describes work, not seniority, credentials, or employer-specific titles.

entries.name: Architects, Except Landscape and Naval
entries.definition: Plan and design structures, such as private residences, office buildings, theaters, factories, and other structural property. Excludes “Landscape Architects” (17-1012) and “Marine Engineers and Naval Architects” (17-2121).

entries.name: Landscape Architects
entries.definition: Plan and design land areas for projects such as parks and other recreational facilities, airports, highways, hospitals, schools, land subdivisions, and commercial, industrial, and residential sites.

entries.name: Cartographers and Photogrammetrists
entries.definition: Research, study, and prepare maps and other spatial data in digital or graphic form for one or more purposes, such as legal, social, political, educational, and design purposes. May work with Geographic Information Systems (GIS). May design and evaluate algorithms, data structures, and user interfaces for GIS and mapping systems. May collect, analyze, and interpret geographic information provided by geodetic surveys, aerial photographs, and satellite data.

entries.name: Surveyors
entries.definition: Make exact measurements and determine property boundaries. Provide data relevant to the shape, contour, gravitation, location, elevation, or dimension of land or land features on or near the earth’s surface for engineering, mapmaking, mining, land evaluation, construction, and other purposes.

entries.name: Aerospace Engineers
entries.definition: Perform engineering duties in designing, constructing, and testing aircraft, missiles, and spacecraft. May conduct basic and applied research to evaluate adaptability of materials and equipment to aircraft design and manufacture. May recommend improvements in testing equipment and techniques.

entries.name: Agricultural Engineers
entries.definition: Apply knowledge of engineering technology and biological science to agricultural problems concerned with power and machinery, electrification, structures, soil and water conservation, and processing of agricultural products.

entries.name: Bioengineers and Biomedical Engineers
entries.definition: Apply knowledge of engineering, biology, chemistry, computer science, and biomechanical principles to the design, development, and evaluation of biological, agricultural, and health systems and products, such as artificial organs, prostheses, instrumentation, medical information systems, and health management and care delivery systems.

entries.name: Chemical Engineers
entries.definition: Design chemical plant equipment and devise processes for manufacturing chemicals and products, such as gasoline, synthetic rubber, plastics, detergents, cement, paper, and pulp, by applying principles and technology of chemistry, physics, and engineering.

entries.name: Civil Engineers
entries.definition: Perform engineering duties in planning, designing, and overseeing construction and maintenance of building structures and facilities, such as roads, railroads, airports, bridges, harbors, channels, dams, irrigation projects, pipelines, power plants, and water and sewage systems. Includes architectural, structural, traffic, and geotechnical engineers. Excludes “Hydrologists” (19-2043).

entries.name: Computer Hardware Engineers
entries.definition: Research, design, develop, or test computer or computer-related equipment for commercial, industrial, military, or scientific use. May supervise the manufacturing and installation of computer or computer-related equipment and components. Excludes “Software Developers” (15-1252) and “Web Developers” (15-1254).

entries.name: Electrical Engineers
entries.definition: Research, design, develop, test, or supervise the manufacturing and installation of electrical equipment, components, or systems for commercial, industrial, military, or scientific use. Excludes “Computer Hardware Engineers” (17-2061).

entries.name: Electronics Engineers, Except Computer
entries.definition: Research, design, develop, or test electronic components and systems for commercial, industrial, military, or scientific use employing knowledge of electronic theory and materials properties. Design electronic circuits and components for use in fields such as telecommunications, aerospace guidance and propulsion control, acoustics, or instruments and controls. Excludes “Computer Hardware Engineers” (17-2061).

entries.name: Environmental Engineers
entries.definition: Research, design, plan, or perform engineering duties in the prevention, control, and remediation of environmental hazards using various engineering disciplines. Work may include waste treatment, site remediation, or pollution control technology.

entries.name: Industrial Engineers, Including Health and Safety
Health and Safety Engineers, Except Mining Safety Engineers and Inspectors
entries.definition: Promote worksite or product safety by applying knowledge of industrial processes, mechanics, chemistry, psychology, and industrial health and safety laws. Includes industrial product safety engineers.

entries.name: Industrial Engineers
entries.definition: Design, develop, test, and evaluate integrated systems for managing industrial production processes, including human work factors, quality control, inventory control, logistics and material flow, cost analysis, and production coordination. Excludes “Health and Safety Engineers, Except Mining Safety Engineers and Inspectors” (17-2111).

entries.name: Marine Engineers and Naval Architects
entries.definition: Design, develop, and evaluate the operation of marine vessels, ship machinery, and related equipment, such as power supply and propulsion systems.

entries.name: Materials Engineers
entries.definition: Evaluate materials and develop machinery and processes to manufacture materials for use in products that must meet specialized design and performance specifications. Develop new uses for known materials. Includes those engineers working with composite materials or specializing in one type of material, such as graphite, metal and metal alloys, ceramics and glass, plastics and polymers, and naturally occurring materials. Includes metallurgists and metallurgical engineers, ceramic engineers, and welding engineers.

entries.name: Mechanical Engineers
entries.definition: Perform engineering duties in planning and designing tools, engines, machines, and other mechanically functioning equipment. Oversee installation, operation, maintenance, and repair of equipment such as centralized heat, gas, water, and steam systems.

entries.name: Mining and Geological Engineers, Including Mining Safety Engineers
Mining and Geological Engineers, Including Mining Safety Engineers
entries.definition: Conduct subsurface surveys to identify the characteristics of potential land or mining development sites. May specify the ground support systems, processes, and equipment for safe, economical, and environmentally sound extraction or underground construction activities. May inspect areas for unsafe geological conditions, equipment, and working conditions. May design, implement, and coordinate mine safety programs. Excludes “Petroleum Engineers” (17-2171).

entries.name: Nuclear Engineers
entries.definition: Conduct research on nuclear engineering projects or apply principles and theory of nuclear science to problems concerned with release, control, and use of nuclear energy and nuclear waste disposal.

entries.name: Petroleum Engineers
entries.definition: Devise methods to improve oil and gas extraction and production and determine the need for new or modified tool designs. Oversee drilling and offer technical advice.

entries.name: Engineers, All Other
entries.definition: All engineers not listed separately. Excludes “Sales Engineers” (41-9031), “Locomotive Engineers” (53-4011), and “Ship Engineers” (53-5031).

entries.name: Drafters, Engineering Technicians, and Mapping Technicians
Architectural and Civil Drafters
entries.definition: Prepare detailed drawings of architectural and structural features of buildings or drawings and topographical relief maps used in civil engineering projects, such as highways, bridges, and public works. Use knowledge of building materials, engineering practices, and mathematics to complete drawings.

entries.name: Electrical and Electronics Drafters
entries.definition: Prepare wiring diagrams, circuit board assembly diagrams, and layout drawings used for the manufacture, installation, or repair of electrical equipment.

entries.name: Mechanical Drafters
entries.definition: Prepare detailed working diagrams of machinery and mechanical devices, including dimensions, fastening methods, and other engineering information.

entries.name: Drafters, All Other
entries.definition: All drafters not listed separately.

entries.name: Engineering Technologists and Technicians, Except Drafters
Aerospace Engineering and Operations Technologists and Technicians
entries.definition: Operate, install, adjust, and maintain integrated computer/communications systems, consoles, simulators, and other data acquisition, test, and measurement instruments and equipment, which are used to launch, track, position, and evaluate air and space vehicles. May record and interpret test data.

entries.name: Civil Engineering Technologists and Technicians
entries.definition: Apply theory and principles of civil engineering in planning, designing, and overseeing construction and maintenance of structures and facilities under the direction of engineering staff or physical scientists.

entries.name: Electrical and Electronic Engineering Technologists and Technicians
entries.definition: Apply electrical and electronic theory and related knowledge, usually under the direction of engineering staff, to design, build, repair, adjust, and modify electrical components, circuitry, controls, and machinery for subsequent evaluation and use by engineering staff in making engineering design decisions. Excludes “Broadcast Technicians” (27-4012).

entries.name: Electro-Mechanical and Mechatronics Technologists and Technicians
entries.definition: Operate, test, maintain, or adjust unmanned, automated, servomechanical, or electromechanical equipment. May operate unmanned submarines, aircraft, or other equipment to observe or record visual information at sites such as oil rigs, crop fields, buildings, or for similar infrastructure, deep ocean exploration, or hazardous waste removal. May assist engineers in testing and designing robotics equipment.

entries.name: Environmental Engineering Technologists and Technicians
entries.definition: Apply theory and principles of environmental engineering to modify, test, and operate equipment and devices used in the prevention, control, and remediation of environmental problems, including waste treatment and site remediation, under the direction of engineering staff or scientists. May assist in the development of environmental remediation devices.

entries.name: Industrial Engineering Technologists and Technicians
entries.definition: Apply engineering theory and principles to problems of industrial layout or manufacturing production, usually under the direction of engineering staff. May perform time and motion studies on worker operations in a variety of industries for purposes such as establishing standard production rates or improving efficiency.

entries.name: Mechanical Engineering Technologists and Technicians
entries.definition: Apply theory and principles of mechanical engineering to modify, develop, test, or adjust machinery and equipment under direction of engineering staff or physical scientists.

entries.name: Calibration Technologists and Technicians
entries.definition: Execute or adapt procedures and techniques for calibrating measurement devices, by applying knowledge of measurement science, mathematics, physics, chemistry, and electronics, sometimes under the direction of engineering staff. Determine measurement standard suitability for calibrating measurement devices. May perform preventive maintenance on equipment. May perform corrective actions to address identified calibration problems. Excludes “Medical Equipment Preparers” (31-9093) and “Timing Device Assemblers and Adjusters” (51-2061).

entries.name: Engineering Technologists and Technicians, Except Drafters, All Other
entries.definition: All engineering technologists and technicians, except drafters, not listed separately.

entries.name: Surveying and Mapping Technicians
entries.definition: Perform surveying and mapping duties, usually under the direction of an engineer, surveyor, cartographer, or photogrammetrist, to obtain data used for construction, mapmaking, boundary location, mining, or other purposes. May calculate mapmaking information and create maps from source data, such as surveying notes, aerial photography, satellite data, or other maps to show topographical features, political boundaries, and other features. May verify accuracy and completeness of maps. Excludes “Cartographers and Photogrammetrists” (17-1021), “Surveyors" (17-1022), and “Geoscientists, Except Hydrologists and Geographers” (19-2042).

sections.title: What distinguishes Architecture and Engineering Occupations
paragraphs: The 2018 Standard Occupational Classification places Architecture and Engineering Occupations in major group 17-0000. Its minor groups include Architects, Surveyors, and Cartographers, Engineers, Drafters, Engineering Technicians, and Mapping Technicians. The hierarchy then distinguishes broad occupations such as Architects, Except Naval, Surveyors, Cartographers, and Photogrammetrists, Aerospace Engineers, Agricultural Engineers, Bioengineers and Biomedical Engineers. Those classifications describe work performed; they do not establish an employer's exact job title, organizational seniority, professional eligibility, or a person's qualifications. Read the official definition at the level that matches the work, and compare it with the employer's written responsibilities.

The detailed records under Architecture and Engineering Occupations span 36 occupations. Their definitions can help candidates and employers discuss the substance of a role when familiar titles are used differently. A useful comparison asks what outputs the person owns, which decisions they make, whom they advise or lead, and what specialized knowledge or credentials are required. A classification is a reference point, not a substitute for the job description or applicable licensing and qualification rules.

Senior positions often combine several kinds of work, while the SOC hierarchy groups occupations by their primary work concepts. A senior leader should therefore explain the actual remit in plain language: functional authority, team or stakeholder relationships, budget or service scope where disclosable, and the evidence behind claimed outcomes. Do not assume that a management title maps to one code or that an individual contributor code indicates limited organizational impact. Validate the occupation against duties and employer context.

Career transitions within Architecture and Engineering Occupations should be tested against the specific minor group and detailed occupations, not just the major-group label. Compare the target duties with examples such as Architects, Except Naval, Surveyors, Cartographers, and Photogrammetrists, Aerospace Engineers, Agricultural Engineers, Bioengineers and Biomedical Engineers, identify the skills and outcomes that transfer, and make any gaps explicit. Where a role has a statutory credential, professional registration, clearance, or jurisdiction-specific requirement, confirm it through the employer and relevant official authority. The SOC source does not certify individual eligibility.

No interview, offer, employment outcome, or timing is guaranteed.

For a practical Architecture and Engineering Occupations search, keep the target job description beside the relevant official definitions and note where the duties agree or differ. Record credential questions separately for confirmation with the employer or relevant authority. This makes the classification useful as a research aid without presenting it as proof of an individual's experience or professional eligibility.

Use major group 17-0000 as the beginning of a role comparison, then move through the official hierarchy until the specific work concept is relevant. When a position spans several specialties, document the primary duties and the additional responsibilities rather than selecting a code from the title alone. This distinction is particularly useful in executive searches, where titles can be broad and authority varies widely. A written comparison keeps the discussion grounded in the work, the evidence, and the requirements confirmed with the prospective employer.

quickFacts.label: Major group title
quickFacts.value: Life, Physical, and Social Science Occupations

entries.name: Life, Physical, and Social Science Occupations
Animal Scientists
entries.definition: Conduct research in the genetics, nutrition, reproduction, growth, and development of domestic farm animals.

entries.name: Food Scientists and Technologists
entries.definition: Use chemistry, microbiology, engineering, and other sciences to study the principles underlying the processing and deterioration of foods; analyze food content to determine levels of vitamins, fat, sugar, and protein; discover new food sources; research ways to make processed foods safe, palatable, and healthful; and apply food science knowledge to determine best ways to process, package, preserve, store, and distribute food.

entries.name: Soil and Plant Scientists
entries.definition: Conduct research in breeding, physiology, production, yield, and management of crops and agricultural plants or trees, shrubs, and nursery stock, their growth in soils, and control of pests; or study the chemical, physical, biological, and mineralogical composition of soils as they relate to plant or crop growth. May classify and map soils and investigate effects of alternative practices on soil and crop productivity.

entries.name: Biochemists and Biophysicists
entries.definition: Study the chemical composition or physical principles of living cells and organisms, their electrical and mechanical energy, and related phenomena. May conduct research to further understanding of the complex chemical combinations and reactions involved in metabolism, reproduction, growth, and heredity. May determine the effects of foods, drugs, serums, hormones, and other substances on tissues and vital processes of living organisms.

entries.name: Microbiologists
entries.definition: Investigate the growth, structure, development, and other characteristics of microscopic organisms, such as bacteria, algae, or fungi. Includes medical microbiologists who study the relationship between organisms and disease or the effects of antibiotics on microorganisms.

entries.name: Zoologists and Wildlife Biologists
entries.definition: Study the origins, behavior, diseases, genetics, and life processes of animals and wildlife. May specialize in wildlife research and management. May collect and analyze biological data to determine the environmental effects of present and potential use of land and water habitats.

entries.name: Biological Scientists, All Other
entries.definition: All biological scientists not listed separately.

entries.name: Conservation Scientists
entries.definition: Manage, improve, and protect natural resources to maximize their use without damaging the environment. May conduct soil surveys and develop plans to eliminate soil erosion or to protect rangelands. May instruct farmers, agricultural production managers, or ranchers in best ways to use crop rotation, contour plowing, or terracing to conserve soil and water; in the number and kind of livestock and forage plants best suited to particular ranges; and in range and farm improvements, such as fencing and reservoirs for stock watering. Excludes “Zoologists and Wildlife Biologists” (19-1023) and “Foresters” (19-1032).

entries.name: Foresters
entries.definition: Manage public and private forested lands for economic, recreational, and conservation purposes. May inventory the type, amount, and location of standing timber, appraise the timber’s worth, negotiate the purchase, and draw up contracts for procurement. May determine how to conserve wildlife habitats, creek beds, water quality, and soil stability, and how best to comply with environmental regulations. May devise plans for planting and growing new trees, monitor trees for healthy growth, and determine optimal harvesting schedules.

entries.name: Epidemiologists
entries.definition: Investigate and describe the determinants and distribution of disease, disability, or health outcomes. May develop the means for prevention and control.

entries.name: Medical Scientists, Except Epidemiologists
entries.definition: Conduct research dealing with the understanding of human diseases and the improvement of human health. Engage in clinical investigation, research and development, or other related activities. Includes physicians, dentists, pharmacologists, and medical pathologists who primarily conduct research. Practitioners who primarily provide medical or dental care or dispense drugs are included in “Healthcare Diagnosing or Treating Practitioners” (29-1000).

entries.name: Life Scientists, All Other
entries.definition: All life scientists not listed separately.

entries.name: Astronomers
entries.definition: Observe, research, and interpret astronomical phenomena to increase basic knowledge or apply such information to practical problems.

entries.name: Physicists
entries.definition: Conduct research into physical phenomena, develop theories on the basis of observation and experiments, and devise methods to apply physical laws and theories. Excludes “Biochemists and Biophysicists” (19-1021).

entries.name: Atmospheric and Space Scientists
entries.definition: Investigate atmospheric phenomena and interpret meteorological data, gathered by surface and air stations, satellites, and radar to prepare reports and forecasts for public and other uses. Includes weather analysts and forecasters whose functions require the detailed knowledge of meteorology.

entries.name: Chemists
entries.definition: Conduct qualitative and quantitative chemical analyses or experiments in laboratories for quality or process control or to develop new products or knowledge. Excludes “Biochemists and Biophysicists” (19-1021) and “Geoscientists, Except Hydrologists and Geographers” (19-2042).

entries.name: Materials Scientists
entries.definition: Research and study the structures and chemical properties of various natural and synthetic or composite materials, including metals, alloys, rubber, ceramics, semiconductors, polymers, and glass. Determine ways to strengthen or combine materials or develop new materials with new or specific properties for use in a variety of products and applications. Includes glass scientists, ceramic scientists, metallurgical scientists, and polymer scientists.

entries.name: Environmental Scientists and Specialists, Including Health
entries.definition: Conduct research or perform investigation for the purpose of identifying, abating, or eliminating sources of pollutants or hazards that affect either the environment or public health. Using knowledge of various scientific disciplines, may collect, synthesize, study, report, and recommend action based on data derived from measurements or observations of air, food, soil, water, and other sources. Excludes “Zoologists and Wildlife Biologists” (19-1023), “Conservation Scientists” (19-1031), “Forest and Conservation Technicians” (19-4071), “Occupational Health and Safety Specialists” (19-5011), “Fish and Game Wardens” (33-3031), and “Forest and Conservation Workers” (45-4011).

entries.name: Geoscientists, Except Hydrologists and Geographers
entries.definition: Study the composition, structure, and other physical aspects of the Earth. May use geological, physics, and mathematics knowledge in exploration for oil, gas, minerals, or underground water; or in waste disposal, land reclamation, or other environmental problems. May study the Earth’s internal composition, atmospheres, and oceans, and its magnetic, electrical, and gravitational forces. Includes mineralogists, paleontologists, stratigraphers, geodesists, and seismologists.

entries.name: Hydrologists
entries.definition: Research the distribution, circulation, and physical properties of underground and surface waters; and study the form and intensity of precipitation and its rate of infiltration into the soil, movement through the earth, and return to the ocean and atmosphere.

entries.name: Physical Scientists, All Other
entries.definition: All physical scientists not listed separately.

entries.name: Economists
entries.definition: Conduct research, prepare reports, or formulate plans to address economic problems related to the production and distribution of goods and services or monetary and fiscal policy. May collect and process economic and statistical data using sampling techniques and econometric methods. Excludes “Market Research Analysts and Marketing Specialists” (13-1161).

entries.name: Survey Researchers
entries.definition: Plan, develop, or conduct surveys. May analyze and interpret the meaning of survey data, determine survey objectives, or suggest or test question wording. Includes social scientists who primarily design questionnaires or supervise survey teams. Excludes “Market Research Analysts and Marketing Specialists” (13-1161) and “Statisticians” (15-2041).

entries.name: Industrial-Organizational Psychologists
entries.definition: Apply principles of psychology to human resources, administration, management, sales, and marketing problems. Activities may include policy planning; employee testing and selection, training, and development; and organizational development and analysis. May work with management to organize the work setting to improve worker productivity.

entries.name: Clinical and Counseling Psychologists
entries.definition: Assess, diagnose, and treat mental and emotional disorders of individuals through observation, interview, and psychological tests. Help individuals with distress or maladjustment understand their problems through their knowledge of case history, interviews with patients, and theory. Provide individual or group counseling services to assist individuals in achieving more effective personal, social, educational, and vocational development and adjustment. May design behavior modification programs and consult with medical personnel regarding the best treatment for patients. Excludes “Psychiatrists” (29-1223).

entries.name: School Psychologists
entries.definition: Diagnose and implement individual or schoolwide interventions or strategies to address educational, behavioral, or developmental issues that adversely impact educational functioning in a school. May address student learning and behavioral problems and counsel students or families. May design and implement performance plans, and evaluate performance. May consult with other school-based personnel.

entries.name: Psychologists, All Other
entries.definition: All psychologists not listed separately.

entries.name: Sociologists
entries.definition: Study human society and social behavior by examining the groups and social institutions that people form, as well as various social, religious, political, and business organizations. May study the behavior and interaction of groups, trace their origin and growth, and analyze the influence of group activities on individual members.

entries.name: Urban and Regional Planners
entries.definition: Develop comprehensive plans and programs for use of land and physical facilities of jurisdictions, such as towns, cities, counties, and metropolitan areas.

entries.name: Miscellaneous Social Scientists and Related Workers
Anthropologists and Archeologists
entries.definition: Study the origin, development, and behavior of human beings. May study the way of life, language, or physical characteristics of people in various parts of the world. May engage in systematic recovery and examination of material evidence, such as tools or pottery remaining from past human cultures, in order to determine the history, customs, and living habits of earlier civilizations.

entries.name: Geographers
entries.definition: Study the nature and use of areas of the Earth’s surface, relating and interpreting interactions of physical and cultural phenomena. Conduct research on physical aspects of a region, including land forms, climates, soils, plants, and animals, and conduct research on the spatial implications of human activities within a given area, including social characteristics, economic activities, and political organization, as well as researching interdependence between regions at scales ranging from local to global.

entries.name: Historians
entries.definition: Research, analyze, record, and interpret the past as recorded in sources, such as government and institutional records, newspapers and other periodicals, photographs, interviews, films, electronic media, and unpublished manuscripts, such as personal diaries and letters.

entries.name: Political Scientists
entries.definition: Study the origin, development, and operation of political systems. May study topics, such as public opinion, political decisionmaking, and ideology. May analyze the structure and operation of governments, as well as various political entities. May conduct public opinion surveys, analyze election results, or analyze public documents. Excludes “Survey Researchers” (19-3022).

entries.name: Social Scientists and Related Workers, All Other
entries.definition: All social scientists and related workers not listed separately.

entries.name: Life, Physical, and Social Science Technicians
Agricultural Technicians
entries.definition: Work with agricultural scientists in plant, fiber, and animal research, or assist with animal breeding and nutrition. Set up or maintain laboratory equipment and collect samples from crops or animals. Prepare specimens or record data to assist scientists in biology or related life science experiments. Conduct tests and experiments to improve yield and quality of crops or to increase the resistance of plants and animals to disease or insects.

entries.name: Food Science Technicians
entries.definition: Work with food scientists or technologists to perform standardized qualitative and quantitative tests to determine physical or chemical properties of food or beverage products. Includes technicians who assist in research and development of production technology, quality control, packaging, processing, and use of foods.

entries.name: Biological Technicians
entries.definition: Assist biological and medical scientists. Set up, operate, and maintain laboratory instruments and equipment, monitor experiments, collect data and samples, make observations, and calculate and record results. May analyze organic substances, such as blood, food, and drugs.

entries.name: Chemical Technicians
entries.definition: Conduct chemical and physical laboratory tests to assist scientists in making qualitative and quantitative analyses of solids, liquids, and gaseous materials for research and development of new products or processes, quality control, maintenance of environmental standards, and other work involving experimental, theoretical, or practical application of chemistry and related sciences.

entries.name: Environmental Science and Protection Technicians, Including Health
entries.definition: Perform laboratory and field tests to monitor the environment and investigate sources of pollution, including those that affect health, under the direction of an environmental scientist, engineer, or other specialist. May collect samples of gases, soil, water, and other materials for testing.

entries.name: Geological Technicians, Except Hydrologic Technicians
entries.definition: Assist scientists or engineers in the use of electronic, sonic, or nuclear measuring instruments in laboratory, exploration, and production activities to obtain data indicating resources such as metallic ore, minerals, gas, coal, or petroleum. Analyze mud and drill cuttings. Chart pressure, temperature, and other characteristics of wells or bore holes.

entries.name: Hydrologic Technicians
entries.definition: Collect and organize data concerning the distribution and circulation of ground and surface water, and data on its physical, chemical, and biological properties. Measure and report on flow rates and ground water levels, maintain field equipment, collect water samples, install and collect sampling equipment, and process samples for shipment to testing laboratories. May collect data on behalf of hydrologists, engineers, developers, government agencies, or agriculture. Excludes “Hydrologists” (19-2043).

entries.name: Nuclear Technicians
entries.definition: Assist nuclear physicists, nuclear engineers, or other scientists in laboratory, power generation, or electricity production activities. May operate, maintain, or provide quality control for nuclear testing and research equipment. May monitor radiation.

entries.name: Social Science Research Assistants
entries.definition: Assist social scientists in laboratory, survey, and other social science research. May help prepare findings for publication and assist in laboratory analysis, quality control, or data management. Excludes “Teaching Assistants, Postsecondary” (25-9044).

entries.name: Forest and Conservation Technicians
entries.definition: Provide technical assistance regarding the conservation of soil, water, forests, or related natural resources. May compile data pertaining to size, content, condition, and other characteristics of forest tracts under the direction of foresters, or train and lead forest workers in forest propagation and fire prevention and suppression. May assist conservation scientists in managing, improving, and protecting rangelands and wildlife habitats. Excludes “Conservation Scientists” (19-1031) and “Foresters” (19-1032).

entries.name: Miscellaneous Life, Physical, and Social Science Technicians
Forensic Science Technicians
entries.definition: Collect, identify, classify, and analyze physical evidence related to criminal investigations. Perform tests on weapons or substances, such as fiber, hair, and tissue to determine significance to investigation. May testify as expert witnesses on evidence or crime laboratory techniques. May serve as specialists in area of expertise, such as ballistics, fingerprinting, handwriting, or biochemistry.

entries.name: Life, Physical, and Social Science Technicians, All Other
entries.definition: All life, physical, and social science technicians not listed separately.

entries.name: Occupational Health and Safety Specialists and Technicians
Occupational Health and Safety Specialists and Technicians
Occupational Health and Safety Specialists
entries.definition: Review, evaluate, and analyze work environments and design programs and procedures to control, eliminate, and prevent disease or injury caused by chemical, physical, and biological agents or ergonomic factors. May conduct inspections and enforce adherence to laws and regulations governing the health and safety of individuals. May be employed in the public or private sector.

entries.name: Occupational Health and Safety Technicians
entries.definition: Collect data on work environments for analysis by occupational health and safety specialists. Implement and conduct evaluation of programs designed to limit chemical, physical, biological, and ergonomic risks to workers.

sections.title: What distinguishes Life, Physical, and Social Science Occupations
paragraphs: The 2018 Standard Occupational Classification places Life, Physical, and Social Science Occupations in major group 19-0000. Its minor groups include Life Scientists, Physical Scientists, Social Scientists and Related Workers, Life, Physical, and Social Science Technicians, Occupational Health and Safety Specialists and Technicians. The hierarchy then distinguishes broad occupations such as Agricultural and Food Scientists, Biological Scientists, Conservation Scientists and Foresters, Medical Scientists, Miscellaneous Life Scientists. Those classifications describe work performed; they do not establish an employer's exact job title, organizational seniority, professional eligibility, or a person's qualifications. Read the official definition at the level that matches the work, and compare it with the employer's written responsibilities.

The detailed records under Life, Physical, and Social Science Occupations span 48 occupations. Their definitions can help candidates and employers discuss the substance of a role when familiar titles are used differently. A useful comparison asks what outputs the person owns, which decisions they make, whom they advise or lead, and what specialized knowledge or credentials are required. A classification is a reference point, not a substitute for the job description or applicable licensing and qualification rules.

Senior positions often combine several kinds of work, while the SOC hierarchy groups occupations by their primary work concepts. A senior leader should therefore explain the actual remit in plain language: functional authority, team or stakeholder relationships, budget or service scope where disclosable, and the evidence behind claimed outcomes. Do not assume that a management title maps to one code or that an individual contributor code indicates limited organizational impact. Validate the occupation against duties and employer context.

Career transitions within Life, Physical, and Social Science Occupations should be tested against the specific minor group and detailed occupations, not just the major-group label. Compare the target duties with examples such as Agricultural and Food Scientists, Biological Scientists, Conservation Scientists and Foresters, Medical Scientists, Miscellaneous Life Scientists, identify the skills and outcomes that transfer, and make any gaps explicit. Where a role has a statutory credential, professional registration, clearance, or jurisdiction-specific requirement, confirm it through the employer and relevant official authority. The SOC source does not certify individual eligibility.

This page includes the complete major-group record and all 5 minor, 25 broad, and 48 detailed records. Detailed occupation definitions come from the official BLS definitions workbook; parent codes follow the BLS structure worksheet sequence rather than an assumed code-prefix rule. This makes the table traceable to both source workbooks and helps distinguish similar titles whose work concepts differ.

For international career planning, map the duties to the relevant local occupational classification rather than assuming that a U.S. SOC code translates directly. Compare the employing entity, target role, actual responsibility, location, work authorization, and credential requirements. Current market evidence should be dated and sourced to official statistics or employer disclosures. The table is not a demand or salary ranking and does not claim that one country has more opportunities than another.

KOV Career Agency provides candidate-side career representation and individual career services. Depending on the written engagement, support may help define target roles, organize evidence, research organizations, and coordinate applications or outreach approved by the professional. Candidates retain approval of external activity; employers retain hiring decisions. Scope, deliverables, fees, and reporting are agreed directly before work begins. No interview, offer, employment outcome, or timing is guaranteed.

For a practical Life, Physical, and Social Science Occupations search, keep the target job description beside the relevant official definitions and note where the duties agree or differ. Record credential questions separately for confirmation with the employer or relevant authority. This makes the classification useful as a research aid without presenting it as proof of an individual's experience or professional eligibility.

Use major group 19-0000 as the beginning of a role comparison, then move through the official hierarchy until the specific work concept is relevant. When a position spans several specialties, document the primary duties and the additional responsibilities rather than selecting a code from the title alone. This distinction is particularly useful in executive searches, where titles can be broad and authority varies widely. A written comparison keeps the discussion grounded in the work, the evidence, and the requirements confirmed with the prospective employer.

sections.title: Candidate-side representation with clear boundaries
paragraphs: KOV works for the professional, not the employer. Depending on agreed scope, candidate-side support may include target definition, organization research, positioning, approved applications, outreach, interview preparation, and offer support. The professional reviews and approves external activity.

Classification codes help organize research but do not establish fit or guarantee an employer response. Engagement scope, deliverables, approvals, fees, and reporting are agreed directly and in writing. KOV does not promise interviews, offers, employment, or timing.

faqs.question: What does SOC major group 19-0000 classify?
faqs.answer: It classifies work concepts in Life, Physical, and Social Science Occupations. The official minor, broad, and detailed hierarchy appears in the directory.

faqs.question: How many detailed occupations are in SOC 19-0000?
faqs.answer: The verified BLS 2018 structure lists 48 detailed occupations under this major group.

faqs.question: Which minor groups fall under Life, Physical, and Social Science Occupations?
faqs.answer: The official minor groups include Life Scientists, Physical Scientists, Social Scientists and Related Workers, Life, Physical, and Social Science Technicians, Occupational Health and Safety Specialists and Technicians. The table lists every minor group and its descendant occupations.

faqs.question: Are SOC 19-0000 codes equivalent to employer job titles?
faqs.answer: No. SOC codes classify work performed; employers may use different titles or combine responsibilities.

faqs.question: Can I use a Life, Physical, and Social Science Occupations code to prove professional eligibility?
faqs.answer: No. The classification is not a credential or eligibility determination. Confirm requirements with the employer and relevant authority.

faqs.question: Does this Life, Physical, and Social Science Occupations page compare job demand across countries?
faqs.answer: No. It provides the U.S. SOC 2018 structure and a market-research checklist, not current vacancy, salary, or demand comparisons.
